entries.title: Federal Immigration Agents Shoot and Wound a Man in New York
entries.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he called President Trump about the incident and hopes to end ICE enforcement actions in the city.
entries.content:
A federal immigration agent shot a man in New York City on Thursday afternoon, city officials said.

The shooting occurred around 4 p.m. in Marble Hill, a Manhattan neighborhood that borders the Bronx, the New York Police Department said in a post on X. The person was conscious and is being treated at a hospital. No NYPD officers were involved or at the scene at the time of the shooting, the department said.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the man and a 5-year-old had been surrounded by agents, though the child was physically unharmed after the altercation. The mayor called the event “unconscionable” and said he had called President Donald Trump about the “incredibly serious situation.”

“I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city,” Mamdani wrote in a post on X.

He ended the post by calling to “abolish ICE.”

Gov. Kathy Hochul wrote in a post on X that she expected federal officials to “provide a full and transparent accounting” of the shooting.

When reached for comment, the NYPD referred The Washington Sun to its earlier post on X. The mayor’s office, the Department of Homeland Security and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

This is a developing story.
entries.author: Manuela Silva

entries.title: Jon Ossoff Accuses Mike Collins of Having ‘Hired Half the Third Reich’
entries.summary: The Democratic senator made his opponent’s staff and family members, who have propagated white supremacist views, a focus of the Georgia Senate debate.
entries.content:
Sen. Jon Ossoff hammered Rep. Mike Collins, his opponent in the Georgia Senate race, over his connections to staff and family members who have propagated white supremacist views.

He called Collins a “bigot” and at one point in the hour-long debate on Thursday said he had “hired half the Third Reich to staff [his] congressional office.”

“Imagine running for the U.S. Senate while neo-Nazi propaganda is disseminated to an audience of millions from your home. That’s Mike Collins,” Ossoff said, referring to Collins’ son-in-law David Alan Scheer II, who reportedly lives on a property owned by Collins.

Collins, who has a history of posting inflammatory posts from his account on X, has been dogged by a string of scandals involving his staff and family members throughout the race, including several who have far-right connections.

Collins fired a chief of staff over the summer following reports that the staffer had been in a group chat with prominent white nationalists, in which the staffer said he was trying to free an imprisoned Holocaust denier. Another former staffer posted Nazi imagery on his personal X account. And a July CNN investigation into Scheer unearthed a history of promoting far-right conspiracy theories online.

Collins has previously issued statements condemning his staffers’ comments but has dodged questions about his son-in-law. When asked by moderators on Thursday to address the issue, Collins suggested that he had spoken with his son-in-law about it.

“I've condemned racism, antisemitism, hate. I don't care where the source is, and I tell him that too,” Collins said, without specifying who he was referring to. “It’s wrong.”

Collins also noted he has fired staffers over their online comments.

Ossoff, who has consistently led in polling and has a massive cash advantage to Collins, repeatedly steered the debate back to those controversies.

Collins blamed the “craziness that Jon Ossoff has been spewing” for an alleged death threat he received, which resulted in the arrest of a man in Buffalo, New York, last week. The suspect was accused of sending death threats to Collins and his son-in-law via Instagram.

In a copy of the arrest warrant obtained by The Washington Sun, deputies alleged the suspect sent a message saying, “Ill come to Jackson and smoke you cracka ass and ya father-in-law.”

National Republican groups in recent weeks have shifted resources away from swing states like North Carolina to defend turf in increasingly competitive red states, such as Kansas and South Carolina, The Sun previously reported.

Collins’ struggles against Ossoff may be precipitating a similar retreat in Georgia. Republicans’ Senate Leadership Fund has canceled nearly $2 million in Georgia ad buys, The Sun reported Thursday.
entries.author: Hunter Riggall

entries.title: The First Debate in Michigan’s Heated Senate Race Was ... Intense
entries.summary: Republican nominee Mike Rogers suggested Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed may have family on a terrorist watch list.
entries.content:
The Michigan Senate debate on Thursday was as heated and personal as the rest of the race has been.

Republican nominee Mike Rogers repeatedly called Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed a “glitchy AI chatbot” and suggested the Muslim American has ties to terrorists. El-Sayed called Rogers cowardly and accused him of going after the “Peeping Tom vote” by supporting local government control of Flock cameras.

The moderator, Rick Albin of WOOD TV8, said after an ad break that the intensity wasn’t limited to on-air time: “In the 30 years of doing debates, I’ve never seen it continue into commercial.”

The Michigan race is one of the most competitive in the country, with the open seat rated as a “toss up” by The Cook Political Report. Winning the seat could be the difference between controlling the U.S. Senate for both Democrats and Republicans.

Each candidate was eager to talk about affordability, which has been a focus for most congressional races across the country. El-Sayed was quick to attach President Donald Trump’s economic track record to Rogers’ “direct line” to the White House, reminding the audience that Rogers has been in Congress before.

“He’s going to make this about him and me,” El-Sayed said, predicting the rest of the debate's tone. “But really, it’s about you and whether you can afford your gas and your groceries.”

Rogers began to address the affordability-concerns question with an answer about a diesel rebate but got off track when he prodded at the legitimacy of El-Sayed’s medical license. El-Sayed received his medical degree from Columbia University and has a doctorate in public health from Oxford University, but Republicans have seized on him having little history of treating patients. El-Sayed is not licensed to practice medicine in Michigan.

“If somebody came into his office and he tried to treat that patient, he’d go to jail,” Rogers said.

El-Sayed threw his fair share of punches, asking Rogers to “just be serious, my guy,” in response to his opponent’s economic policy. Later on, El-Sayed called Rogers “my guy” again; Rogers shot back by calling El-Sayed “brother.”

Artificial intelligence and data centers have been hot topics throughout the Michigan race, with both candidates calling for some level of regulation on the technology. El-Sayed is running on public ownership of AI companies and regulation of Flock surveillance technology by the federal government. Rogers has advocated for a temporary moratorium on data centers and supports letting local governments control Flock cameras, but he said he doesn’t approve of them being misused.

El-Sayed launched an anti-Flock ad blitz earlier this week, which included a website with blown-up photos of Rogers’ face with “Mike Rogers is watching you” underneath.

The quips grew more personal when Rogers said Flock cameras could be used to catch terrorists.

“Why would that bother you?” Rogers said. “Well, if you have somebody in your family that might be on the watch list …”

El-Sayed jumped in and dared his opponent to finish his sentence.

“Go ahead and say it,” El-Sayed said. “You’ve been tiptoeing around it.”

Rogers then brought up El-Sayed’s birth mother, who’s been accused of working for a group designated as a terrorist organization. At another point in the debate, Rogers suggested El-Sayed has relationships to groups like Hamas, Hezbollah and Al-Qaeda. These allegations have been reported to be misleading by the Detroit Free Press, and El-Sayed’s campaign has not yet commented on the allegation about his biological mother.

In Rogers’ closing pitch, he warned that El-Sayed was not the right choice to represent Michigan, only mentioning himself in his final seconds.

“We cannot afford Abdul, and we cannot risk his ideology,” Rogers said.

El-Sayed similarly focused on Rogers in his final 30 seconds, although he tried to circle back to his starting message about focusing on Michiganders.

“I told you what this debate was going to be: him pointing at me and saying all kinds of foreign names, or him talking about himself,” El-Sayed said.

A post-debate camera angle showed Rogers leaning over to El-Sayed for a quick handshake before disappearing offstage. The candidates are expected to be back on the debate stage Oct. 21 in Detroit.

entries.title: House Republican Campaign Chief Launches Defensive Spending in His Own Race
entries.summary: The ad reservations made by North Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson suggest he’s being cautious about his own reelection.
entries.content:
Rep. Richard Hudson, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has reserved tens of thousands of dollars in TV ad buys in his North Carolina district as Republicans fight to hold onto their slim majority.

The ad buys are striking because Hudson, tasked with protecting the Republican House majority, represents a district that President Donald Trump won by more than 15 percentage points in 2024. The rocky political climate for Republicans has members in solid red seats taking very few chances ahead of the midterm elections.

A source with access to an ad tracking database told The Washington Sun that Hudson’s campaign had reserved north of $200,000 in spending. Federal Communications Commission records verified a flurry of activity by Hudson’s campaign in the tens of thousands of dollars this week.

Hudson’s campaign did not dispute the $200,000 figure.

“Congressman Hudson runs hard every cycle, and this one is no different. He was on air at home in 2022, he was on air in 2024, and he's on air now. He earns every vote, every time,” said Cam Mills, Hudson’s campaign manager, in a statement.

His team did not provide documentation suggesting past cycle spending was comparable to the spending his campaign is doing now.

In one 30-second spot, Hudson, sitting at a bar counter, speaks against stock trading by members of Congress and name-checks former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi.

A Democratic-leaning pollster surveyed the race last month and found Hudson leading Democrat Richard Ojeda, 46% to 42%.

“I think this may be a recognition that some Republicans who would have felt comfortable not having to advertise, not having to do massive campaigning are probably seeing some writing on the wall of Democratic enthusiasm,” Michael Bitzer, professor of politics at Catawba College, told The Sun of the spending. “This may be an attempt just to shore up their walls around their district.”

Hudson, who as chair of the NRCC spends a lot of time traveling and fundraising, hasn’t faced a competitive challenger since 2020, when Patricia Timmons-Goodson came within 6 percentage points. Odeja previously served in the West Virginia state Senate.

“RICHARD HUDSON IS ON TV. WE NEED TO BE TOO,” Ojeda’s campaign posted on Facebook on Thursday in a fundraising plea.

Ojeda’s campaign reported raising $2.2 million compared to Hudson’s $3.2 million as of the end of June.

The “ad buy does not mean that the ship's going down, but it does mean that they're having to pay attention to it,” Chris Cooper, professor of political science at Western Carolina University told The Sun.

Hudson’s ad spend also reflects broader Republican anxiety over North Carolina.

This summer, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee moved Hudson’s district to its “districts in play” list, though The Cook Political Report still categorizes the district as solid Republican.

North Carolina is also the setting of a competitive Senate race between Democrat Roy Cooper and Republican Michael Whatley, which is drawing national attention and could have implications for the House races in the state.

“If Republicans are less likely to show up because they're not fired up about Whatley, then that's going to hurt Republicans downballot,” Cooper said.

A recent AARP poll shows Cooper leading Whatley by 11 percentage points.

Last week, the Republican Senate Leadership Fund pulled out of the state in favor of spending in Kansas and South Carolina. The Raleigh News & Observer reported Wednesday that Whatley had paused his ads in order to rethink strategy.
entries.author: Kadia Goba, Chase Pellegrini de Paur

entries.title: D.C. Schools May Soon Have a Big Problem: Fewer Kids
entries.summary: Birth rates are down and enrollment is flat, meaning tough questions could lie ahead.
entries.content:
Earlier this week, each and every one of D.C.’s public and charter schools did something relatively unspectacular: They counted their kids.

Routine as it may be, the annual count is critical, helping D.C. officials determine exactly how many kids are enrolled citywide. And since funding is attached to enrollment, the count is how D.C. calculates how much money each school will get for the year.

This year, though, the count may count for more.

Relatively flat enrollment in D.C.’s public and charter schools last year is raising concerns that the city may soon face the same downward trend that other states, counties and cities have started experiencing, largely because of declining birth rates but also decreases in the number of families coming into the system or choosing to stay.

While officials and experts say there’s no immediate crisis, they add that a possible decline in enrollment — after almost 15 years of steady increases — would prompt difficult and uncomfortable questions and policy choices. That could include potentially closing schools, a route Maryland’s Montgomery County is considering.

“We are in a situation where we should be looking at these trends, because we don’t want to get to a point where we're at a low and don’t have policies to address it,” said Anoosha Imran, an education research analyst with the D.C. Policy Center, a local think tank.

Minus a brief dip during the pandemic, enrollment in D.C. schools has steadily increased over the last two decades, jumping from some 71,280 students in DCPS and charter schools in the 2008-09 school year to 99,555 students in 2024-25.

That largely tracks with the years that D.C.’s economy and population boomed, as did births. Those peaked in 2016, when 9,854 D.C.-resident children were born. But it’s been a steady decline since then, and in 2025 only 7,318 such births were recorded in the city.

“We watch that number particularly carefully, and birth rates become a very important part of our long-term projections because they go through the system,” said Paul Kihn, D.C.’s deputy mayor for education.

The lower birth rates are playing out most clearly in the earlier grades in D.C. schools, notably in the number of families enrolling their kids in pre-K for 3- and 4-year-olds, which has been free in D.C. since 2009. According to data from Kihn’s office, enrollment in pre-K dropped 3 percent from the 2024-25 school year to 2025-26. And there are hints it might continue: The number of applications for schools through D.C.’s universal lottery tool hit 20,987 this year, down from 23,312 two years ago.

In the past, people moving into D.C. could offset the decreases in local births, but that has recently changed — in large part because of federal immigration policies. And those same policies may have contributed to one of the biggest enrollment decreases D.C. schools saw in the 2025-26 school year: Latino students, whose enrollment fell 3.8%.

Kihn said it’s too early to panic; he hopes if any enrollment declines occur this school year, they are gentle. “But if it's something bigger than that, then that would be concerning,” he said.

If the enrollment decline picks up steam, city officials and experts agree it could prompt difficult decisions about whether to keep certain schools open — especially as the city’s budget is getting leaner. Those conversations would likely initially focus on schools that are already underenrolled. According to an annual assessment of school utilization across D.C., 18 DCPS schools and 15 charter schools are under 50% enrolled relative to their capacity.

“It’s hard to operate schools that are significantly underenrolled. It can be harmful for the rest of the District. It’s also bad for those students. How do you provide those students with robust services if you only have 200 to 300 students? It’s very expensive to have a nurse, it’s very expensive in high school to have a range of AP courses,” said Chad Aldeman, an educational analyst and consultant, speaking this week during a conference organized by the D.C. Policy Center.

But closing underenrolled schools would pose challenges. Many are in Wards 7 and 8, where incomes and educational indicators have lagged other parts of D.C. Additionally, past rounds of school closures — 23 in 2008 and 13 in 2013 — targeted a number of DCPS schools in those neighborhoods.

Responding to Aldeman, Kaya Henderson, who was DCPS chancellor from 2010 to 2016 and oversaw one round of school closures, argued that any future decisions on closing schools have to be based on more than just raw enrollment numbers.

“I want to resist the frame that let’s just look at places that are underenrolled and cut there, because over in Wards 7 and 8 those kids need a more robust educational infrastructure than potentially kids in Ward 3. That’s just our reality,” she said.

Kihn said that as decisions like these approach, DCPS and charters — which operate independently from each other — will have to cooperate and coordinate, something that historically hasn’t happened between two sectors that were set up to compete.

“What you don't want is if you lose thousands of kids, for example, and then you've got DCPS over here making some decisions about how they should respond and you've got the charter sector over here making some decisions,” he said. “What you want to have is a coherent citywide approach.”

Officials and experts say that D.C. shouldn’t just assume the inevitability of school enrollment dropping and the difficult responses that would require, but also find ways to encourage families to remain in the city. That includes continuing to invest in the city’s schools, which have seen gains in test scores and achievement, while also taking steps to make D.C. more affordable for families.

“When you look at things like how expensive it is to raise a child in the District when your average cost of early learning is $26,000 a year on top of some of the most expensive rent in the country, it is hard to have and grow a family in the District,” said Joanna Blotner, government affairs director for D.C. Action, which advocates for kid-friendly policies. “All of those things need to be taken into consideration.”

Blotner said D.C. should continue pushing to expand the supply of child care and bring down its cost, something that Ward 4 Council member Janeese Lewis George, who is likely to be the city’s next mayor, has said she will focus on.

“If we have folks who are investing in enrolling their kids in early-learning programs and seeing the District as family-friendly,” Blotner said, “they’re more likely to want to stay in the District long-term.”

entries.title: Major Unions and Business Groups Clash Over Defense Contractor Stock Buybacks
entries.summary: The fight pits organized labor against corporate America as Congress and the president push defense firms to prioritize arms production.
entries.content:
The United Auto Workers, Teamsters, United Steelworkers and four other major unions are urging Congress to restrict stock buybacks and dividends by defense contractors, wading into a fight over how weapons makers spend billions of dollars in taxpayer revenue.

The unions are backing a provision in the Senate’s defense policy bill that is opposed by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other major business groups, pitting organized labor against corporate America over efforts in Congress and the Trump administration to push weapons companies to invest more in arms production. Business groups warn the move would set a precedent for federal overreach into private industry

The fight has scrambled traditional political alliances. Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts), Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) and Mike Lee (R-Utah) championed the Senate provision, while President Donald Trump has also targeted defense contractor stock buybacks, dividends and executive compensation. In a January executive order, Trump directed the Pentagon to restrict those payments at contractors deemed to be underperforming or making weapons too slowly.

The provision would bar the Pentagon from awarding contracts to companies that repurchase shares, pay dividends or make other capital distributions, unless the defense secretary grants a waiver tied to a qualifying defense investment plan.

In a letter sent this week to leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services committees, the unions urged lawmakers to preserve Section 815 of the Senate’s 2027 National Defense Authorization Act as the chambers negotiate a final version of the bill. The unions say they represent millions of workers, including those at major defense contractors and their suppliers.

The unions argue the industry is shortchanging workers on pay while rewarding shareholders with billions in stock buybacks and dividends.

“The working class makes the defense industry run, but instead of investing in our national and economic security, companies like Lockheed Martin, Boeing, Woodward, and dozens more spend taxpayer dollars on Wall Street payoffs to enrich the billionaires,” UAW President Shawn Fain said in a statement.

The unions pointed to Trump’s actions as evidence Congress should go further.

Warren, Hawley and Lee have said the five largest defense contractors have spent more than $100 billion on stock buybacks and dividends since 2020 — more than twice what they spent on capital expenditures. The unions said spending on buybacks and dividends by major defense contractors fell 36% after Trump’s executive order, which they say shows the restrictions are workable.

The unions said labor disputes and work stoppages over the past two years at Boeing, Lockheed, General Dynamics, Textron, GE Aerospace and Pratt & Whitney show that the industry’s spending priorities are leaving its workforce behind.

The U.S. Chamber and more than 40 other business and industry groups previously urged lawmakers to strip Section 815 from the Senate bill, warning that the restrictions would discourage companies from doing business with the Pentagon just as the government is trying to attract new suppliers and private investment into the defense industry.

In a July letter to Senate Armed Services Committee leaders, the groups argued that stock buybacks and dividends benefit millions of Americans who hold shares directly or through retirement accounts. They also warned that the restrictions could hurt employees whose stock ownership plans rely on dividend payments, and they disputed the idea that companies are sacrificing investment in production to reward shareholders.

The business groups also warned that the restrictions would give Washington unprecedented influence over corporate financial decisions, setting a precedent that could extend well beyond the defense industry.

“By prohibiting dividends, share repurchases, and other capital distributions absent a government waiver, Section 815 would shift responsibility for ordinary capital allocation decisions from corporate leadership to Washington,” the groups wrote.
